question: After an immutable release and its tag are deleted, can a documented public read-only GitHub surface distinguish a tag name that was never used from the same currently-absent tag name that was previously reserved by an immutable release?

histories.A_never_used: Repository is in current state S; candidate tag name T has never backed an immutable release; no current ref T, release T, or attestation T exists.
histories.B_used_then_deleted: Repository is restored to the same current state S; T previously backed a published immutable release; that release was deleted and then its tag was deleted; no current ref T, release T, or attestation T exists. GitHub nevertheless documents that T cannot be reused, including after repository resurrection.

documented_read_projection.A: 404 when ref T does not exist

documented_read_projection.B: no exact current ref T after deletion
deleted immutable release object is absent from the current-release projection, as bounded in Part98
deleted/unfindable attestation state after release deletion, as bounded in Part98

method.hidden_state_oracle: A mutating attempt to reuse T can distinguish the histories because GitHub documents permanent non-reuse of an immutable-release tag name after release deletion and even repository resurrection. This is a service-side write-time oracle, not a documented non-mutating read-visible floor.

observations: GitHub documents that an immutable release locks its associated tag while the release exists; after deleting the release the tag may be deleted, but the same tag name cannot be reused.
GitHub further documents that this non-reuse survives repository deletion and recreation with the same name.
GitHub's documented Get-a-reference endpoint returns 404 when the requested ref does not exist; therefore it exposes only current ref existence, not the hidden immutable-release reservation history.
The bounded documentation search for immutable-release, release-by-tag, and Git-ref read surfaces did not surface a documented read-only endpoint that returns the hidden used-tag reservation state.
inferences: Within the four tested current read projections, histories A and B are observationally indistinguishable even though a later mutating reuse attempt has different behavior.

The immutable-tag reservation therefore remains useful as a write-time duplicate/replay fence for the exact previously-used tag name, but it is not established as a stateless read-visible monotonic freshness floor.

This does not prove that no undocumented or future GitHub endpoint can expose the reservation state; the negative claim is limited to the bounded documented surfaces searched in this leaf plus the Part98 predecessor surfaces.

source_qualification.supports: tag cannot be deleted while immutable release exists; after release deletion tag can be deleted but same tag name cannot be reused; protection survives repository resurrection

source_qualification.source: GitHub Docs: REST API endpoints for Git references
source_qualification.supports: Get a reference exposes current Git ref and returns 404 when ref does not exist; list-matching-refs exposes current refs

result.falsified_candidate: Treat GitHub immutable-release tag-name non-reuse as a documented stateless read-visible minimum-generation/freshness floor after the release/tag are deleted.
result.preserved_mechanism: Exact-name immutable-release non-reuse remains a documented write-time stale-replay/duplicate fence for names that have already been used.
result.minimal_unresolved_child: A read-visible, non-mutating, monotonic incarnation/generation witness that survives deletion/recreate, or a sink-side minimum-generation rule that rejects stale generations without relying on a mutating probe or an external coordinator.

zero_dependency_zero_quota_assessment.repository_api_role: read-only/public documentation and lightweight repository transport evidence only; no hosted compute or finite-credit mechanism accepted

scope_guard: Only the two constructed histories, four documented current-read projections, the bounded GitHub documentation search performed on 2026-09-01, and the Part98 predecessor findings. No universal claim about undocumented internals, future endpoints, or arbitrary external sinks.
